h1: Brewpub opening hours and staff shifts that make money
title: Brewpub Opening Hours and Staff Shifts | Craft Beer School
desc: How to set brewpub opening hours and staff shifts from your own sales data, so labour cost tracks demand and slow hours stop draining money.
teaser: Every hour your doors are open costs money. Some hours earn it back. Your POS already knows which.
standfirst: Labour is one of the biggest costs in a brewpub and the easiest to waste. Opening hours and shift patterns built from your own sales data, rather than habit, can cut cost without hurting service. Here is a method.
sections:
Your POS can export sales by hour and by day. Pull at least eight weeks, ideally including a festival period and a quiet one. For each hour, look at revenue, number of bills and covers. Most brewpubs find a clear shape: quiet weekday afternoons, a build from early evening, a peak in the late evening and strong weekend lunches. Your shape may differ, which is the point of looking.

Our guide to POS and inventory software for brewpubs covers getting clean data out.

The most useful single number is revenue per labour hour: sales in a period divided by the staff hours worked in it. Calculate it by hour of day and day of week. Low numbers show where you are overstaffed or open when nobody comes. High numbers can show where service suffers because you are understaffed. Track labour cost as a share of sales over each week as well. Decide your own target from your margins.

Our guide to weekly numbers for brewpub owners shows how to fit this into a simple dashboard.
Opening hours: rules first, then data

Permitted hours for serving alcohol are set by your state and sometimes by local authorities. They can differ for weekdays, weekends and dry days. Start with what is allowed, then decide what makes sense inside it. Check the current rules for your licence category.

Within the permitted window, ask whether each block of hours pays for its staff, power and air conditioning. A brewpub that opens at noon on weekdays may find the first three hours barely cover the lights. Opening at 4 PM on weekdays and noon at weekends can serve the same guests with fewer dead hours. Test changes for a month and compare.

• Stagger start times. Bring servers in as the evening builds rather than all at opening.
  • Split shifts are common in Indian hospitality for lunch and dinner. They work, but they are tiring. Use them carefully and give staff proper rest.
  • Part-time staff for peaks. Weekend evenings and festival weeks often need extra hands that weekdays do not.
  • Cross-train. A server who can run the bar or a bartender who can help on the floor smooths out peaks.
  • Schedule cleaning and prep for quiet hours, so peak hours are for guests.

Your state's shops and establishments rules set limits on working hours, overtime, weekly offs and, in some cases, late working. Follow them and keep records. Our guide to brewery staffing covers roles and team size.
The brewhouse runs on a different clock

Brewing does not follow guest hours. Brew days often start early so the boil and cooling finish before service. Fermentation checks happen every day, including days the taproom is closed. Plan brewer shifts around the production calendar, not the bar rota. Keep noisy work such as milling and cleaning-in-place out of service hours where the layout puts the brewhouse in view of guests.

Demand in India moves with weather, exams, festivals and cricket. Summer and the festive season can be very different from the monsoon. Plan rosters for each season rather than one pattern all year. Our guide to planning a brewpub year around Indian seasons maps the typical pattern.

Start from forecast covers for each hour, not from last month's roster. Decide how many guests one server can look after well at peak and how many bills the bar can handle. Divide forecast demand by those numbers to get the staff you need hour by hour, then build shifts to cover that shape with as few short or broken shifts as possible. Publish rosters at least a week ahead so staff can plan their lives. Teams that know their hours stay longer. Staff turnover is expensive in training time alone.
Fill slow hours or close them

For each slow block, choose: fill it or close it. Filling it might mean a weekday lunch menu, a quiz night, a tasting session or a corporate booking. Check your state's rules before running drink promotions, as some restrict them. If nothing fills it after a fair test, close those hours and put the saved labour into service at peak.

Our guide to taproom economics shows how small changes in labour and covers move the bottom line.
